item.title: The Trump Administration Is Trying to Keep College Students From Voting. Don’t Let It.
item.description:
When America lowered the voting age from 21 to 18, the move had broad bipartisan support, starting with college students and civil rights groups and running right up through Congress and state legislatures. At the 26th Amendment’s signing ceremony, 55 years ago last month, President Richard Nixon declared that “America’s new voters, America’s young generation,” would bring “moral courage” and “a spirit of high idealism” to the country.

Today, however, America’s current “young generation” — and in particular, college students — stand at the intersection of two of the Trump administration’s favorite targets: voting rights and higher education. Through a range of measures, the administration has sought to make it more difficult for students to vote and for colleges and universities to assist student voters.

The connection between education and democracy has been core to American ideals since the nation’s founding. Thomas Jefferson, who went on to found the University of Virginia, wrote, “No other sure foundation can be devised, for the preservation of freedom and happiness.” For this historical reason — and more practically, because college students may live away from home — institutions of higher learning have traditionally made an effort to facilitate registration and voting.

The Trump administration’s new regulations are aimed right at those efforts. If universities do not fight to maintain the vital work they have done to promote democracy in its most literal form, they will lose that foundational purpose, and the nation will lose the vital contributions of countless young adults.

Last August, just as the academic year was beginning, the Department of Education sent a “Dear Colleague” letter to college administrators informing them that their institutions could no longer use federal work-study funds to support nonpartisan civic activities such as voter registration, voter hotlines and voter assistance at polling places. These are activities that groups such as the ALL IN Campus Democracy Challenge and the Students Learn Students Vote Coalition have shown demonstrably increase student voter turnout.

The message in the latest edition of the Federal Student Aid Handbook appears to set a somewhat less restrictive standard. So what exactly is permissible? The American Council on Education encourages institutions to “assess from their own risk vantage point.”

Helping students vote should not require nerves of steel.

New regulations that could go into effect as early as Oct. 1, just over a month before the 2026 midterms, would place even greater restrictions on this activity. The Office of Management and Budget has proposed to classify voter registration efforts by colleges and other nonprofit organizations, even if nonpartisan, as “lobbying,” and therefore to ban the use of any federal grant dollars for that purpose or “related activities.” We can only speculate about the rationale for this change, because the O.M.B. failed to provide the justification that is required by law.

The attacks on college-based voter registration efforts don’t just limit healthy democratic engagement; they violate the spirit of our existing federal law. The 1998 reauthorization of the Higher Education Act requires colleges and universities to make a “good faith” effort to provide their students with voter registration materials.

In addition, laws in states such as California, Maryland, Minnesota and Michigan require proactive measures to encourage student voting. Depending on how these new federal regulations are interpreted, they might come into conflict with the state laws, too.

In February, Secretary of Education Linda McMahon declared that “American colleges and universities should be focused on teaching, learning and research — not influencing elections.” Her statement was made in a news release about a federal investigation into the National Study of Learning, Voting and Engagement, a nonpartisan research project that for 13 years has helped educators understand and promote civic participation at more than 1,000 colleges and universities.

Neither the study nor Tufts, the study’s home, has been accused of any wrongdoing, but the threat of sanctions — against both the National Student Clearinghouse, the source of essential data for the study, and the schools that participate in the project — appears to have been enough to halt research for the foreseeable future.

The paradox is that Ms. McMahon, along with many other members of the Trump administration and a growing number of voices on both sides of the political divide, champions a return to civics education. But the purpose of that education does not end at the classroom door.

Its value is in its ability to get people involved in civic life and the democratic process. That’s precisely the goal of these college activities and organizations, yet they are coming under relentless attack.

American colleges and universities must not be neutral on the issues of democracy and civic participation. Institutions should do what they have been doing since before the Declaration of Independence: educate students and help shape them as informed and engaged citizens.

In the 2022 midterms, only 31.3 percent of college students voted. We should all view this as unacceptable. College leaders should articulate their opposition to the proposed rule changes and find resources to promote and defend the most foundational of democratic rights. This is not a question of partisanship but of citizenship.

This month, when first-year students arrived at Bard College, where for 15 years I have directed the Center for Civic Engagement, they all had to visit a voter registration booth even before they received their room keys. No one was required to register, but several hundred did, and those who were already registered and planning to vote from home received help with the often complex absentee ballot process.

Instead of shying away from this legitimate activity, colleges should redouble their efforts to reach young people, educate them and assist them as they navigate the registration and voting process. They should not just teach students about their democratic rights; they should help students realize them. There is no truer way to fulfill their educational mission.

Jonathan Becker is the acting president of Bard College and an editor of “Youth Voting Rights: Civil Rights, the Twenty-Sixth Amendment, and the Fight for American Democracy on College Campuses.”

item.title: Mamdani Sues City Council Over $10,000 Bonuses to Teachers’ Aides
item.description:
Mayor Zohran Mamdani sued the New York City Council on Wednesday, arguing that its bill granting hefty bonuses to some of the city’s lowest-paid school workers violates collective bargaining law, a city spokesman said.

The decision to sue comes the same day that the City Council bill became law, after the mayor declined to issue a veto, knowing that the Council had the votes to override it.

The suit, filed in State Supreme Court in Manhattan, could set the scene for the mayor’s highest-profile fight so far with a public sector union and stands to embitter his already fraught relationship with the Council’s speaker, Julie Menin, who championed the legislation.

But a spokesman for the mayor said the city was acting to protect labor rights.

“We will not allow the political process to replace the collective bargaining table,” said the spokesman, Matt Rauschenbach. “The city is filing a lawsuit to protect the right of every union to negotiate on behalf of its members, to fight for the workplace they deserve and ensure that workers — not politicians — determine their own futures.”

The Council bill, backed by the influential United Federation of Teachers, would grant $10,000 bonuses to New York City teaching assistants, who often work one-on-one with children with disabilities and are among the worst-paid workers in the city’s public school system.

Mr. Mamdani, a democratic socialist who often closely aligns himself with organized labor, supported the bonuses on the campaign trail, but came out against them once he became mayor. He argued that the bill violated state and city labor law, which requires such issues to be hammered out via collective bargaining.

The teachers’ union backed Mr. Mamdani for mayor only after he won the Democratic primary last summer.

Mr. Rauschenbach said the administration was committed to raising paraprofessional pay by other means.

“We want to engage in productive conversations with the U.F.T. to permanently address this inequity,” he said.

The mayor, who campaigned on the promise of making New York more affordable for all, now finds himself in the politically awkward position of fighting the teachers’ union and potentially blocking bonuses for low-income city employees who work with vulnerable children.

Nor is Ms. Menin’s position without political complications. The speaker often casts herself as a more fiscally moderate foil to the mayor, but the legislation she has championed would, according to critics, amount to an expensive end-run around collective bargaining that other unions would be eager to emulate.

As evidence, opponents of the legislation note that Joann Ariola, the councilwoman who chairs the Committee on Fire and Emergency Management, recently pointed to the paraprofessional bonuses in her request to raise the pay for the Fire Department’s emergency medical technicians, some of whom make as little as $18 an hour.

In an interview on Wednesday morning on “The Brian Lehrer Show” on WNYC, Ms. Menin said that it made fiscal sense to fund the bonuses and help fill paraprofessional job vacancies, at a time when the city is spending more than $1 billion a year to send children with disabilities to private schools where they can receive more specialized services.

“Every member of the Council, in a unanimous and bipartisan vote, supported the RESPECT Check Act because it is unacceptable that paraprofessionals who support some of our highest-need students are earning as little as $32,000 a year,” said Ms. Menin on Wednesday afternoon, in a joint statement with Carmen De La Rosa, the councilwoman who sponsored the legislation.

The first tranche of the bonuses is not due until Jan. 1.

The ambiguity surrounding the legislation’s future did not stop the teachers’ union from declaring victory.

In an email to paraprofessionals on Wednesday, Michael Mulgrew, the union’s president, wrote, “Today, the RESPECT check became law! All of our hard work has gotten us to this moment. As of today, paraprofessionals can expect to receive their first RESPECT payment in January.”

Mr. Mulgrew had threatened “all-out war” on the mayor if he tried to block the legislation.

In an interview on Wednesday, Mr. Mulgrew said the city’s claim that it was suing to protect workers was “a joke.”

“The lowest-paid workers in my union, majority Black and brown women, you’re trying to stop them from getting this check, good luck with that,” he said, adding that he was somewhat encouraged that Mr. Mamdani had become more personally involved in this issue in recent weeks.

The roughly 26,000 paraprofessionals who work in New York’s public school system, America’s largest, have a starting salary of about $32,000 a year.

The legislation would cost an estimated $325 million, according to the nonpartisan Citizens Budget Commission, a watchdog group.

The commission, and the mayor’s allies, also warned that the law threatened to sow havoc in the city’s half-century-old collective bargaining practices, by establishing a precedent that when unions did not get what they wanted at the bargaining table, they could just turn to the City Council for help.

Robert W. Linn, who worked as the city’s labor relations commissioner under Mayor Bill de Blasio and continues to advise City Hall under Mr. Mamdani, said that the state and city labor laws had been put in place to stop the chaos that typified collective bargaining in the 1960s, when there were strikes by teachers, social service workers and sanitation workers.

“There are almost 150 bargaining units in New York City,” Mr. Linn said. “If you don’t have a rigorous collective bargaining approach, then parties are going to be running to the City Council, to the State Legislature, they’re going to be engaging in work stoppages. I think there is the potential to return to that chaos.”
